column2: There is one hater and no second beyond him, who dwells in the heart; I speak of him. Instructed by that teacher always, all the serpents, hated by the world, were defeated.
On this too they cite an ancient tale: the discussion between Prajapati, the serpents and the divine sages.
Divine sages, nagas and asuras, sitting by Prajapati, asked: "Tell us what is best for us."
To them who asked what was best the blessed one said the one-syllable Brahman, "Om"; hearing it, they ran off in all directions.
For those running off, the disposition to bite arose among the serpents first, for the instruction of themselves.
Having reached one teacher, refined by one word, all of them, serpents, gods, sages and danavas, settled on various ends.
He hears what is said and takes it as it is; to one who asks so much more, another teacher consents.
With his consent the act then goes forward; the teacher, the knower, the enemy and the hater are lodged in the heart.
Wandering in the world with sin, one becomes a doer of sin; wandering with good, he becomes a doer of good.
One who delights in sensual pleasure is a free-liver by desire; one who delights in conquering the senses is ever a keeper of vows.
One who, free of vows and rites, relies solely on Brahman, wandering the world as Brahman-become, is a celibate student.
Brahman alone is his fuel, Brahman the fire, Brahman the seat; water is Brahman, the teacher is Brahman; he is concentrated in Brahman.
This subtle celibacy of such a kind the wise know; having known it they attained it, shown by the knower of the field.
[Brahmin] "I have crossed the road that is the one passage beyond objects, that obstructs desire and anger; having crossed that great difficulty I have entered a great forest."
[Brahmin woman] "Where is that forest, greatly wise one, what trees and rivers are in it, what mountains, and how far along the road is it?"
[Brahmin] "In separateness there is nothing else equal to it; in non-separateness there is nothing farther than it.
There is nothing lower than it and nothing greater than it; there is nothing more sorrowful than it, and no other happiness equal to it.
Having entered it, the twice-born neither grieve nor rejoice; they fear none, and none fears them.
In that forest are seven great trees, seven fruits, seven guests, seven hermitages, seven concentrations and seven consecrations: this is the form of the forest.
Trees there put forth divine flowers and fruits of five colours and stand pervading that forest.
Trees there put forth flowers and fruits of gold and of two colours and stand pervading that forest.
Two great trees, putting forth many flowers and fruits of unmanifest colours, stand pervading that forest.
One fire is there, a well-minded brahmin; the five senses are the fuel; from them liberations arise, seven consecrations; the qualities are the fruits, the guests and the hopes of fruit.
There the seven great sages accept hospitality; when they have been honoured and have dissolved, another forest pleases.
A tree of vow without fruit, with the shade of peace, resting on knowledge, with the water of contentment and the sun that is the knower of the field within.
The good who reach it have no fear again; above, below and across, its end is not found.
Seven women dwell there at once, downward-faced, radiant, mothers; above, they give the essences to creatures, all as all, and impermanence.
There the seven sages are established and rise again, the perfected, with Vasishtha at their head.
Glory, splendour, fortune, victory, perfection and radiance: so the seven lights follow the sun.
Mountains and hills are there in short, and rivers and streams, bearing waters that are born of Brahman.
There is the confluence of rivers, the Vaitana, near by, whence the self-satisfied, self-controlled go directly to the Grandsire.
Of slight desire and good vows, their sins burned by austerity, placing the Self in the Self, they worship Brahma.
Those who know the forest of knowledge also recite a verse about it, intending that forest, how the steadfast was born.
Brahmins know such a divine forest as this; having known it they practised it, as shown by the knower of the field."
[Brahmin] "Nature desires the wished objects; nature hates all the disliked; desire and hatred arise from nature, placing prana and apana in the bodies of creatures.
I would discern in the body, apart from them and among them, the impermanent states and the self of beings; standing in it I cannot be touched at all by desire, anger, old age and death.
For one who does not desire all desires and does not hate all faults, no stains attach in my natures, like a drop of water on lotus leaves.
For this eternal one who looks at many natures, the net of enjoyment does not cling in actions, like the net of the sun's rays in the sky.
On this too they cite an ancient tale; learn it, famous lady: the discussion between an Adhvaryu and an ascetic.
Seeing a victim being sprinkled in a sacrificial rite, the ascetic seated there said to the Adhvaryu, reproaching: "I would kill."
The Adhvaryu replied to him: "This goat does not perish; the creature will be joined to a better state if so the scripture says.
Its earthly part will go to the earth, and whatever of it is born of water will go to the waters."
[Ascetic] "If you see good for the goat in separation from its life-breaths, then the sacrifice is for the goat's sake; what is your purpose?
Let mother, father, brother and friend consent to you; take counsel with the goat, lifting it up, especially when it speaks.
You should ask those who would consent, and having heard their consent you can then deliberate.
The vital breaths of this goat have gone into their own wombs; only the body remains, motionless, in my opinion.
Violence with a body like fuel, by one without understanding: for those who wish to be free of it, the victim is called fuel.
Non-harm is the first of all dharmas, so say the aged; we hold that the deed that is without harm should be done.
If I declare non-harm as my vow, much can be said against your act.
Non-harm to all beings always pleases us; we accomplish what is before us and do not attend to the unseen."
[Adhvaryu] "You enjoy the qualities of smell from earth, drink the tastes made of water, see the form of lights, touch the qualities born of wind,
hear the sound born of space, and think with the mind. You think all these are beings, life-breaths.
You are constant in taking life, and you engage in harm; there is no activity without harm. What do you think, brahmin?"
[Ascetic] "Imperishable and perishable: this self is twofold. The imperishable is being; the perishable is called nature.
Prana, tongue, mind, goodness, nature with passion: for one freed of these states, free of dualities, free of hopes,
equal to all beings, without possessiveness, self-conquered, released on all sides, there is no fear anywhere."
[Adhvaryu] "Association should be with the good here, best of the wise. Hearing your view, my mind is enlightened.
Blessed one, awakened by your blessed understanding, I speak: I am not at fault in thinking, acting or doing, brahmin."
[Brahmin] Then the ascetic, with that reasoning, remained silent, and the Adhvaryu too, free of delusion, went on in the great sacrifice.
Brahmins know such subtle liberation, and having known it they practise it, shown by the knower of the field.
There was a king named Kartavirya Arjuna with a thousand arms, by whom the earth to the sea was conquered with the bow.
Once, wandering at the sea's edge, proud of his strength, he covered the sea with hundreds of arrows, so we have heard.
The ocean, saluting him with folded hands, said: "Do not loose arrows, hero; tell me what I may do for you.
Creatures dependent on me are being killed by the great arrows you loose, tiger among kings; give them safety, lord."
[Arjuna] "If anyone bearing a bow is equal to me in battle, tell me of him who could stand against me in fight."
[Ocean] "If you have heard of the great sage Jamadagni, his son is fit to give you proper hospitality."
Then the king set off, filled with great anger; coming to that hermitage he fell upon Rama.
He and his kinsmen did hostile things to Rama and caused trouble to the great soul Rama.
Then some kshatriyas, having killed Jamadagni, entered mountain fastnesses, like deer harried by lions.
Out of fear of them, they did not perform their own appointed duties; the people, not seeing brahmins, fell to the state of low-born.
These Dravidas, Kashas, Pundras and Shabaras fell into low-born state by rising up from kshatriya dharma.
Then, when the kshatriya women's heroes were slain again and again, kshatriyas were born through brahmins, and Jamadagni's son cut them down.
At the end of twenty-one such slaughters a divine bodiless voice, sweet and heard by all the worlds, spoke to Rama:
Rama, Rama, turn back. What merit do you see, dear one, in parting these kshatriya wretches from life again and again?
So too Richika and the other forefathers said to that great soul, "Fortunate one, turn back."
But Rama, not forgiving his father's slaying, said to those sages, "You should not hold me back here."
[Ancestors] "You should not kill the kshatriyas, best of conquerors; it is not fitting for you, a brahmin and good man, to kill kings."
There was a royal sage named Alarka, of great austerity, knower of dharma, true to his word, a great soul of great vows.
Having conquered this earth to the sea with the bow and done a very hard deed, he set his mind on the subtle.
As he stood at the root of a tree, this thought came to him, after giving up a very great kingdom, toward the subtle, O wise one.
[Alarka] "Strength has arisen in my mind; conquering the mind is certain victory. I shall shoot arrows elsewhere, when surrounded by enemies.
Because this mind wishes to do all this out of the restlessness of the body, I shall loose very sharp-pointed arrows at the mind."
[Mind] "These arrows will not pierce me at all, Alarka; they will pierce your own vital spots, and with your vital spots pierced you will die.
Look to other arrows with which you will kill me." Hearing it, he reflected and then said:
[Alarka] "Having smelled many scents, it hankers after those very ones; therefore I shall loose sharp arrows at the nose."
[Nose] "These arrows will not pierce me at all, Alarka; they will pierce your own vital spots, and with your vital spots pierced you will die.
Look to other arrows with which you will kill me." Hearing it, he reflected and then said:
[Alarka] "Having created varied touches, it hankers after those very ones; therefore I shall tear the skin with varied heron-feathered arrows."
[Skin] "These arrows will not pierce me at all, Alarka; they will pierce your own vital spots, and with your vital spots pierced you will die.
Look to other arrows with which you will kill me." Hearing it, he reflected and then said:
[Alarka] "Having heard varied sounds, it hankers after those very ones; therefore I shall loose sharp arrows at the ear."
[Ear] "These arrows will not pierce me at all, Alarka; they will pierce your own vital spots, and then you will lose your life.
Look to other arrows with which you will kill me." Hearing it, he reflected and then said:
[Alarka] "Having seen varied states, it hankers after those very ones; therefore I shall loose sharp arrows at the eye."
[Eye] "These arrows will not pierce me at all, Alarka; they will pierce your own vital spots, and with your vital spots pierced you will die.
Look to other arrows with which you will kill me." Hearing it, he reflected and then said:
[Alarka] "This many-formed resolve is decided by wisdom; therefore I shall loose sharp arrows at the intellect."
[Eye] "These arrows will not pierce me at all, Alarka; they will pierce your own vital spots, and with your vital spots pierced you will die."
[Ancestors] Then Alarka, taking up terrible, very hard austerity, did not find, with all his power, another arrow for these seven; with a concentrated mind the lord then reflected.
Having reflected a long time, O best of brahmins, Alarka, best of the wise, found no higher good than yoga.
Making his mind one-pointed and standing steady in yoga, the mighty one quickly struck down the senses with a single arrow.

Entering the Self by yoga, he went to supreme perfection; and the amazed royal sage sang this verse: "Ah, what pain, that we earlier practised kingship! Afterward I learned that there is no happiness higher than yoga."
Know this too, Rama, and do not kill kshatriyas; take up terrible austerity, and then you will gain the good.
[Brahmin] So addressed by his forefathers, Jamadagni's son took up terrible austerity, very fortunate, and went to hard-to-reach perfection.
Grief, anger and excessive agitation are held to be the passionate qualities; sleep, drowsiness and delusion, those three, are the dark qualities.
Having cut these down with showers of arrows, the steadfast, tireless one, calm in soul and master of his senses, can conquer enemies.
On this, those who know the ancient age recite verses sung by King Ambarisha while ruling the kingdom.
When faults had risen and the good were being slain, Ambarisha seized the kingdom by force, it is heard.
Having subdued the great faults and honoured the good, he went to great perfection and sang this verse:

I have conquered most faults and killed all enemies; one fault remains, to be killed, and I have not killed it.
mahabharata:14:31.8	Joined to it, this creature does not attain freedom from thirst, running like one parched toward low ground and not understanding.
mahabharata:14:31.9	Cut down with sharp swords the greed by which a man, impelled, does here even what should not be done.
So the verse was sung by the renowned King Ambarisha, who, putting sovereignty first, cut down greed alone.
King Janaka said to a brahmin who was in distress about some text, "Do not live in my domain," for his instruction.
Thus addressed, the brahmin replied to the best of kings: "Tell me, O king, the extent of your domain over which you stand in control.
I wish to live in another king's domain, lord; I wish to do your word as the scriptures say, lord of the earth."
Thus addressed by the renowned brahmin, the king sighed again and again hotly and did not reply to him.
As the king of immeasurable power sat meditating, a faintness suddenly came upon him, as Rahu seizes the sun.
Then the king, consoled, when the faintness had passed, spoke to the brahmin after a moment:

In my ancestral kingdom, with the country under my control, searching this whole earth I do not find a domain.
mahabharata:14:32.9	When I did not find it on earth, I searched Mithila; when I did not find it there, I searched my own subjects.
mahabharata:14:32.14	[Janaka] All undertakings here are known to end in all actions; I did not find that which would be 'mine'.
'Whose is this? Whose is the property?' So says the Veda. I did not find by understanding that which would be 'mine'.
Having settled this understanding, I have given up possessiveness. Hear the understanding by which everywhere is my domain.
I do not desire for myself even the smells that reach the nose; therefore the earth, conquered by me, always stays in my control.
I do not desire for myself tastes that are in my mouth; therefore the waters, conquered by me, always stay in my control.
I do not desire for myself form and light by the eye; therefore light, conquered by me, always stays in my control.
I do not desire for myself touches that rest on the skin; therefore wind, conquered by me, always stays in my control.
I do not desire for myself sounds that reach the ear; therefore sounds, conquered by me, always stay in my control.
I do not desire for myself the mind within the mind; therefore the mind, conquered by me, always stays in my control.
All these undertakings are for the gods, ancestors, beings and guests."
Then the brahmin, laughing, said again to Janaka: "Know that I have come here today as Dharma, to test you.
You alone are the mover of this wheel, whose navel is Brahman, whose spokes are the understanding that does not turn back, whose rim is goodness, and which is held still."
Whatever creatures there are in the world, moving and unmoving, know me as the ender of them, as fire is of wood.
This understanding knows kingdom over all the earth or in heaven; understanding is my wealth.
There is one path of the brahmins by which the knowers of that go: in houses, forest dwellings, teachers' houses and among mendicants, by many unagitated signs, one understanding is attended.
Those whose minds are calm, though they stand in various signs and stages, reach one state, as rivers reach the sea.
This path is travelled by understanding, not by the body; actions have beginning and end, and the body is the bond of action.
Therefore, fortunate one, you have no fear for the next world; devoted to my state of being, you will reach my very Self."
[Brahmin] "Know the brahmin woman as the lower fire-stick and the teacher as the upper fire-stick; when austerity and learning are rubbed together, the fire of knowledge is born."
[Brahmin woman] "This mark of Brahman, called the knower of the field: how can it be grasped, and where is its sign?"
[Brahmin] "It is without mark and without qualities, and has no cause; I shall tell only the means by which it may or may not be grasped.
Though rightly taught, it is seen like bees; by lack of understanding, action and understanding rest as if on marks of knowledge.
'This is to be done, this not' is not taught in liberations; understanding arises in those who see and hear for the self.
As many parts as can be here, so many he should imagine, manifest and unmanifest, by hundreds and thousands,
all endowed with plurality, all with perception as their reason; beyond which there is nothing, there he will be in practice."
[Vasudeva] On this too they cite an ancient tale: the conversation about liberation of a pupil with his teacher.
A wise pupil asked a brahmin teacher of strict vows, who was sitting, something about the highest good, scourge of foes.
Blessed one, I have come to you for refuge, devoted to the highest good. I ask you with bowed head, brahmin: explain to me what I should say.
To the pupil who spoke thus, Partha, the teacher said, "Tell me, and I shall tell you where your doubt lies, brahmin."
So addressed, best of the Kurus, the pupil, devoted to his teacher, asked with folded hands; hear it, wise one.
[Pupil] "From where am I, and from where are you? Tell me that truth which is highest. From where are beings born, immovable and moving?
By what do beings live, and what is their lifespan like? What is truth, what austerity, brahmin? What virtues are declared by the good? What paths are auspicious? What is happiness, and what is evil?
Tell me these questions truly, blessed best of men; you should rightly explain here the truth, sage of brahmins."
[Vasudeva] To that pupil, who had come and rightly asked, endowed with virtue, calm, devoted to his teacher, like a shadow, self-controlled, an ascetic and celibate,
the wise, firm-vowed teacher, Partha, answered all those questions rightly, best of the Kurus, scourge of foes.
[Teacher] This dharma, declared as Brahman, served by the best of sages, to be obtained by the Veda's knowledge, making real the truth of things,
the decision about past, future and present, dharma, desire and wealth, known to hosts of the perfected, ancient and eternal,
I shall tell you today, greatly wise one, the supreme state, understanding which the wise here become perfected.
Long ago the sages, wishing to know from each other, Brihaspati, Bharadvaja, Gautama, Bhargava,
Vasishtha, Kashyapa, Vishvamitra and Atri, having travelled all the paths, tired by their own deeds,
putting the aged sage Angirasa before them, saw Brahma, free of sin, in Brahma's abode.
Bowing to that great soul, sitting at ease, the great sages, with humility, asked this supreme highest good:

How should action be done well, how may one be freed from sin? What paths are auspicious for us? What is truth, and what is evil?
mahabharata:14:35.20	By what are the two paths of action, by what does one gain greatness, and what are dissolution and liberation, the origin and end of beings?
What the great-grandsire said, so addressed by the best of sages, I shall tell you, pupil; hear it as the tradition has it.
[Brahma] From truth beings were born, immovable and moving; they live by austerity; know this, you of good vows.
Coming again to their own wombs, they go on by their own deeds. Truth, joined with qualities, is fixed and has five marks.
Truth is Brahman, truth is austerity, truth is Prajapati; from truth beings were born, and this great being is truth.
Therefore brahmins, relying on truth, always devoted to yoga, beyond the heat of anger, restrained, are the bridges of dharma.
I shall tell you of those knowers, mutually bound, who set going the bridges of dharma, eternal makers of the worlds.
The knowledge of the four Vedas, the four classes, and the four stages are separate; dharma is one, four-footed, the wise say, eternal.
I shall tell you the path, twice-born, auspicious and giving safety, fixed for becoming Brahman, walked before by the wise.
Listen, greatly fortunate ones, entire, to the path hard to know that I now tell, higher than the highest.
They say the stage of the celibate student is the first step, the householder's the second, the forest-dweller's next; and after that the supreme step is to be known as the spiritual.
Light, space, the sun, wind, Indra and Prajapati: as long as one does not reach the spiritual, so long he does not see these. I shall tell you the means to it; learn it first.
For sages living in the forest on fruit, roots and air, the forest-dweller's life is taught for the three twice-born classes.
The householder's life is ordained for all classes; faith is its mark, so the steadfast declare of dharma.
These are the paths of the gods declared to you, the bridges of dharma, practised by the good and steadfast by their actions.
One of strict vows who follows dharma in each of these sees in time the origin and dissolution of beings always.
Now I shall tell the principles truly, by reason, as they stand in objects, all present in their portions.
The great self and the unmanifest, and the ego, the ten senses and the eleventh, the five great elements,
the five specific objects of the elements: so says the Vedic tradition. These twenty-four principles have been told to you.
The steadfast one who knows the origin and dissolution of all principles does not come to delusion among beings.
One who knows the principles as they are, and all the qualities and all the deities, shaking off sin and freeing himself from bondage, attains all the stainless worlds.
The eleven-fold circle: the mind, whose essence is working things out, with the intellect as its master, is the highest eleventh.
The three streams that are fed again and again in it, those three channels, move as consisting of the qualities.
Darkness, passion and goodness they call the qualities; all are mutually coupled and mutually live on one another.
They depend on one another and follow one another, mixed together: the three qualities and the five elements.
The couple of darkness is goodness; the couple of goodness is passion; passion's partner is goodness, and goodness's partner is darkness.
Where darkness is restrained, passion goes on; where passion is restrained, goodness goes on.
Know darkness as of the nature of night, threefold, called delusion, marked by unrighteousness, fixed in sinful acts.
They say passion is of the nature of activity, causing alternation, seen in all beings, marked by origination.
The nature of these qualities will be told by reasons and non-reasons, in brief and in detail; learn them truly.
Bewilderment, ignorance, non-renunciation, indecision about acts, sleep, stiffness, fear, greed, grief, disparagement of good deeds,
forgetfulness, non-ripening, unbelief, divided conduct, lack of distinction, blindness, conduct of base qualities,
pride in what is not done, pride of knowledge in ignorance, unfriendliness, distorted mind, faithlessness, deluded thought,
dishonesty, senselessness, sinful action, unconsciousness, heaviness, dejection, blackness and speechlessness:
all these qualities, brahmins, are called dark, and whatever other fixed states in this world are called delusion.
They are all restrained here and there, those dark qualities: constant tales of slander against the gods, brahmins and the Veda.
You should be heedful in every way, delight of the Kurus, in the eightfold kingdom, tiger among kings, with dharma placed first.
When Dhananjaya has departed, the ocean will swiftly flood this city with its ramparts and watchtowers.
The rakshasas who were Duryodhana's allies are named; in due order, O king, they attained all the unsurpassed worlds.
